title: Kinematics-Driven Gaussian Shape Deformation for Blurry Monocular Dynamic Scenes
claim: Standard methods leave primitives misaligned and blurry under motion; aligning them with the velocity direction yields sharp, consistent shapes.
layout: 2 side-by-side photo panels with legends below, motion arrows overlaid
description: Two side-by-side real photographs of a tabletop scene with a red dice-shaped cushion in the centre. A green cube and a blue cube move at left and right. The left panel is labelled 'Standard 3DGS'. In it, the moving cubes are heavily smeared. Large translucent ellipses lie across the blur and are misaligned with the long green and blue motion arrows. The right panel is labelled 'Ours'. Here the green and blue cubes are crisp. Many small white ellipses sit along the motion arrows, and a black arrow marked 'v' shows the estimated velocity. Beneath the panels are legends. The left legend shows overlapping elongated green and blue ellipses, captioned 'Misaligned Gaussian with blurred shape'. The right legend shows compact round green and blue dots, captioned 'Sharp shape Gaussian aligned with motion'. The eye goes first to the blurry versus sharp cubes.
caption: Comparison between standard 3D Gaussian Splatting and our method under motion blur. Our approach aligns Gaussian primitives with the estimated velocity direction $v$, producing sharp and physically consistent shapes. Arrows indicate motion direction, while ellipses visualize Gaussian anisotropy.
abstract: Reconstructing dynamic 3D scenes from blurry monocular videos is challenging as motion-induced blur entangles object motion and geometry, hindering geometric consistency. We present Kinematics-GS, a kinematics-aware framework that models blur as motion-aligned deformation and introduces a kinematic prior to reparameterize Gaussian shapes along motion trajectories, thereby mitigating degenerate shape collapse without auxiliary motion supervision. To stabilize optimization, we decompose scenes into dynamic and static components using temporal deformation variance and employ a coarse-to-fine deformation strategy to capture both global motion and fine-grained details. We also introduce a challenging real-world dataset of deformable and elastic objects exhibiting non-rigid motion with spatially non-uniform motion blur that obscures geometric cues. Extensive experiments on real-world benchmarks with realistic motion blur demonstrate that Kinematics-GS outperforms prior methods by a clear margin in monocular dynamic scene reconstruction, highlighting its effectiveness in handling complex and non-rigid motion scenarios.
